modules.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

cards.front: What is the distinction between Data, Data Structures, and an Abstract Data Type (ADT)?
cards.back:
• Data: Raw, unorganized facts or values.
• Data Structure: A specialized mathematical/logical format for organizing, storing, retrieving, and manipulating data efficiently.
• ADT: A mathematical model defined solely by its data behavior and set of operations from the user's perspective, completely independent of implementation details.
cards.formula_or_code: ADT = Set of Values + Set of Operations

cards.front: Differentiate between Linear vs Non-Linear and Static vs Dynamic Data Structures with examples.
cards.back:
• Linear: Elements form a sequential chain where every element has unique predecessor & successor (except ends). Examples: Arrays, Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists.
• Non-Linear: Multilevel or hierarchical relationships without single sequential order. Examples: Trees, Graphs.
• Static: Fixed memory allocated at compile-time (Array).
• Dynamic: Memory allocated/deallocated at runtime on Heap (Linked List).
cards.formula_or_code: Linear: Array, Stack, Queue, SLL | Non-Linear: Trees, Graphs

cards.front: State the 5 mandatory criteria that an algorithm must satisfy according to Donald Knuth.
cards.back:
1. Input: Zero or more quantities externally supplied.
2. Output: At least one quantity produced.
3. Definiteness: Each instruction must be clear, unambiguous, and precise.
4. Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps for all inputs.
5. Effectiveness: Every instruction must be basic enough to be carried out on paper.
cards.formula_or_code: Criteria: Input, Output, Definiteness, Finiteness, Effectiveness

cards.front: Define Space Complexity and explain its two components.
cards.back:
Total memory required by an algorithm to execute to completion:
S(P) = c + S_p(I)
• Fixed Component (c): Memory independent of input size (instruction space, simple variables, constants).
• Variable Instance Component (S_p(I)): Memory dependent on input instance I (dynamic memory, recursion stack space, dynamically sized data structures).
cards.formula_or_code: S(P) = c + S_p(I)

cards.front: Define Big-O, Big-Omega (Ω), and Big-Theta (Θ) asymptotic notations with mathematical conditions.
cards.back:
• Big-O (Upper Bound / Worst Case): f(n) = O(g(n)) if ∃ constants c > 0, n0 ≥ 1 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
• Big-Omega (Lower Bound / Best Case): f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if ∃ c > 0, n0 ≥ 1 such that 0 ≤ c·g(n) ≤ f(n) for all n ≥ n0.
• Big-Theta (Tight Bound / Average Case): f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if ∃ c1, c2 > 0, n0 ≥ 1 such that c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) for all n ≥ n0.
cards.formula_or_code: Hierarchy: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!)

cards.front: Give the Row-Major and Column-Major memory address formulas for 2D array element A[i][j].
cards.back:
For 2D array A[0..R-1][0..C-1] with element size w bytes and Base Address BA:
• Row-Major Order (Row by row): Address(A[i][j]) = BA + [ i × C + j ] × w
• Column-Major Order (Column by column): Address(A[i][j]) = BA + [ j × R + i ] × w
cards.formula_or_code: Row-Major: BA + (i*C + j)*w | Col-Major: BA + (j*R + i)*w

cards.front: What is a Sparse Matrix? Describe its 3-Tuple representation.
cards.back:
• Definition: A matrix where the vast majority of elements are ZERO. Storing as a standard 2D array wastes memory and computational cycles.
• 3-Tuple Representation: Stored in a compact array of rows [row, col, value].
  - Row 0 (Metadata): [total_rows, total_cols, total_non_zero_elements].
  - Rows 1..k: [r, c, val] for each non-zero element in row-major order.
cards.formula_or_code: Row 0: [Rows, Cols, NonZeros] | Row i: [Row_idx, Col_idx, Value]

cards.front: Compare Simple Transpose vs Fast Transpose of a Sparse Matrix in terms of time and space complexity.
cards.back:
• Simple Transpose: For each column (0 to cols-1), scans all N non-zero elements to place them in transposed order. Time: O(C × N). Space: O(1) auxiliary.
• Fast Transpose: Precomputes two auxiliary arrays:
  1. row_terms[col]: counts non-zero elements per column.
  2. starting_pos[col]: computes starting index in transposed matrix.
  Places each element in exact position in a single pass. Time: O(C + N). Space: O(C) auxiliary.
cards.formula_or_code: Simple: O(C * N) | Fast: O(C + N) with row_terms & starting_pos

cards.front: Define Stack ADT, its operations, and state the Overflow & Underflow conditions in array implementation.
cards.back:
• Stack: LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) linear list where insertions and deletions happen only at one end (TOP).
• Operations: Push (insert), Pop (delete), Peek (inspect top).
• Array Implementation (size MAX, top initialized to -1):
  - Overflow Condition: top == MAX - 1 (cannot push onto full stack).
  - Underflow Condition: top == -1 (cannot pop from empty stack).
cards.formula_or_code:
Push: if(top==MAX-1) Overflow; else arr[++top]=val;
Pop: if(top==-1) Underflow; else return arr[top--];

cards.front: How do you implement Two Stacks in a Single Array efficiently without artificial boundary collisions?
cards.back:
• Array arr[0..MAX-1] with two pointers:
  - Stack 1 grows from left to right: top1 initialized to -1 (Push: ++top1).
  - Stack 2 grows from right to left: top2 initialized to MAX (Push: --top2).
• Underflow:
  - Stack 1: top1 == -1
  - Stack 2: top2 == MAX
• Overflow Condition: top1 + 1 == top2 (occurs only when entire array is completely full).
cards.formula_or_code: Overflow: top1 + 1 == top2

cards.front: State the algorithm rules for converting an Infix expression to Postfix using an operator stack.
cards.back:
1. Initialize operator stack.
2. Scan infix token left-to-right:
   - If Operand: Append directly to postfix output.
   - If '(': Push to stack.
   - If ')': Pop and append from stack until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If Operator (op): While stack is non-empty and precedence(stack[top]) ≥ precedence(op) (for left-associative), pop and append. Then push op onto stack.
3. After scanning, pop all remaining operators from stack to output.
cards.formula_or_code: Precedence: ^ (R-to-L) > *, / (L-to-R) > +, - (L-to-R)

cards.front: How does an Operand Stack evaluate a Postfix arithmetic expression?
cards.back:
1. Initialize operand stack.
2. Scan postfix expression from left-to-right:
   - If Operand: Push value onto stack.
   - If Operator (op): Pop top two operands (op2 = pop(), op1 = pop()). Compute result = op1 [op] op2. Push result back onto stack.
3. Final result is the single element remaining on stack.
(Critical: Second popped element is LEFT operand; first popped is RIGHT operand!).
cards.formula_or_code: op2 = pop(); op1 = pop(); push(op1 [op] op2);

cards.front: What is the False Overflow problem in a Linear Queue, and how does a Circular Queue solve it?
cards.formula_or_code: Circular Full: (rear + 1) % MAX == front | Empty: front == rear

cards.front: Define Double-Ended Queue (Deque) variants and Priority Queue.
cards.back:
• Deque (Double-Ended Queue): Linear list where insertion and deletion can occur at BOTH ends (front and rear).
  - Input-Restricted Deque: Insertion at one end only; deletion at both ends.
  - Output-Restricted Deque: Deletion at one end only; insertion at both ends.
• Priority Queue: Queue where each element has an assigned priority. Elements are dequeued based on priority (highest priority first), regardless of arrival order.
cards.formula_or_code: Deque: Insert/Delete at Front & Rear | Priority Queue: Highest priority served first

modules.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

cards.front: Define a Singly Linked List (SLL) node in C and compare array vs linked list memory allocation.
cards.formula_or_code: Node* n = (Node*)malloc(sizeof(Node)); n->data = val; n->next = NULL;

cards.front: Give the C pointer statements for SLL Insertion and Deletion at Head.
cards.formula_or_code:
Insert Head: newNode->next=head; head=newNode;
Delete Head: temp=head; head=head->next; free(temp);

cards.front: Write the 3-pointer in-place algorithm to reverse a Singly Linked List.
cards.formula_or_code: 3-Pointers: prev=NULL, curr=head, next=NULL; curr->next=prev

cards.front: How are dynamic Stacks and Queues implemented using a Linked List?
cards.back:
• Dynamic Stack:
  - Push: Insert at Head (top) → O(1)
  - Pop: Delete from Head (top) → O(1)
  - Underflow: top == NULL
• Dynamic Queue:
  - Enqueue: Insert at Tail (rear) using rear pointer → O(1)
  - Dequeue: Delete from Head (front) using front pointer → O(1)
  - Underflow: front == NULL
cards.formula_or_code: Stack: Push/Pop at Head | Queue: Enqueue at Tail, Dequeue at Head

cards.front: Describe Doubly Linked List (DLL) node structure and its advantages over Singly Linked List.
cards.formula_or_code: DLL Node: prev (pointer), data, next (pointer)

cards.front: Why is representing a Circular Linked List (CLL) with a single LAST pointer superior to using a HEAD pointer?
cards.back:
• If represented with HEAD: Finding the tail requires traversing all n nodes (O(n)).
• If represented with LAST pointer:
  - Tail node is directly accessible: last (O(1)).
  - Head node is directly accessible: last->next (O(1)).
  - Insertion at beginning: newNode->next = last->next; last->next = newNode; (O(1)).
  - Insertion at end: newNode->next = last->next; last->next = newNode; last = newNode; (O(1)).
cards.formula_or_code: CLL with LAST: Head = last->next (O(1)) | Tail = last (O(1))

cards.front: Compare First-Fit, Best-Fit, Worst-Fit, and Next-Fit dynamic storage allocation schemes.
cards.back:
• First-Fit: Allocates the FIRST free memory hole large enough. Fast, leaves residual fragments at beginning.
• Best-Fit: Searches entire free list to find the SMALLEST hole ≥ requested size. Minimizes wasted space per allocation, but creates many tiny unusable fragments.
• Worst-Fit: Searches entire free list to allocate the LARGEST available hole. Leftover fragment is large and often reusable, but destroys large memory blocks.
• Next-Fit: Variant of First-Fit; starts searching from location of previous allocation.
cards.formula_or_code: First-Fit: Fastest | Best-Fit: Smallest fitting | Worst-Fit: Largest hole

cards.front: Differentiate between Internal Fragmentation and External Fragmentation with causes and remedies.
cards.back:
• Internal Fragmentation: Memory allocated to a process is slightly larger than requested. The unused portion inside the allocated partition is wasted.
  - Cause: Fixed partitioning or block-size rounding.
• External Fragmentation: Total free memory across the system is sufficient to satisfy a request, but the memory is fragmented into non-contiguous scattered holes.
  - Cause: Dynamic variable-block allocation and deallocation.
  - Remedy: Memory Compaction / Paging.
cards.formula_or_code: Internal: Wasted inside block | External: Wasted between blocks

cards.front: Explain the Mark-and-Sweep garbage collection algorithm and Memory Compaction.
cards.back:
• Mark-and-Sweep GC:
  1. Mark Phase: Starts from Root Set (stack variables, globals), traverses all reachable objects via pointer graph, setting a 'visited/marked' bit = 1.
  2. Sweep Phase: Scans the entire heap linearly. Unmarked objects (bit = 0) are garbage collected and returned to free pool; marked bits are reset to 0.
• Memory Compaction: Relocates all live surviving objects to one contiguous end of the heap, updating all reference pointers, producing a single large contiguous free memory block.
cards.formula_or_code: Phase 1: Mark reachable from roots | Phase 2: Sweep unmarked to free list

cards.front: State the key mathematical properties of Binary Trees (max nodes at level i, max nodes in height h, min height with n nodes).
cards.back:
1. Max nodes at level i (root at level 0): 2^i
2. Max nodes in a binary tree of height h: 2^(h+1) - 1
3. Min height with n nodes: h_min = ceil(log2(n+1)) - 1
4. Strict / Full Binary Tree: Nodes have either 0 or 2 children.
5. Complete Binary Tree: All levels filled except possibly last (nodes pushed left).
6. Perfect Binary Tree: All interior nodes have 2 children, all leaves at same level.
cards.formula_or_code: Max nodes at level i = 2^i | Max nodes in height h = 2^(h+1) - 1

cards.front: Prove that in any non-empty binary tree, the number of leaf nodes (n0) is one more than the number of degree-2 nodes (n2): n0 = n2 + 1.
cards.back:
Let n = total nodes, e = total edges.
1. Every edge points to a child, so e = n - 1.
2. In terms of node degrees (n0, n1, n2):
   e = 0·n0 + 1·n1 + 2·n2 = n1 + 2·n2.
3. Equating:
   n - 1 = n1 + 2·n2
4. Since n = n0 + n1 + n2:
   (n0 + n1 + n2) - 1 = n1 + 2·n2
   n0 - 1 = n2  ⇒  n0 = n2 + 1  ■
cards.formula_or_code: Theorem: n_0 = n_2 + 1

cards.front: Define Inorder, Preorder, Postorder, and Level-Order traversals of a Binary Tree.
cards.back:
• Inorder (L-N-R): Traverse Left Subtree → Visit Node → Traverse Right Subtree (Sorted order in BST).
• Preorder (N-L-R): Visit Node → Traverse Left Subtree → Traverse Right Subtree (Used for copying/prefix expressions).
• Postorder (L-R-N): Traverse Left Subtree → Traverse Right Subtree → Visit Node (Used for tree deletion/postfix evaluation).
• Level-Order: Breadth-first level-by-level traversal using a FIFO Queue.
cards.formula_or_code: Inorder: LNR | Preorder: NLR | Postorder: LRN | Level-Order: Queue

cards.front: Why is Inorder traversal MANDATORY to uniquely reconstruct a binary tree along with Preorder or Postorder?
cards.back:
• Preorder/Postorder indicates the Root node (first in Preorder, last in Postorder), but cannot distinguish whether remaining elements belong to the left or right subtree.
• Inorder establishes the boundary: finding the root in Inorder divides elements into Left Subtree (elements to the left of root) and Right Subtree (elements to the right of root).
• Preorder + Postorder CANNOT construct a unique tree (ambiguity arises with single-child nodes).
cards.formula_or_code: Unique Tree = Inorder + Preorder OR Inorder + Postorder

cards.front: What is an Expression Tree and how is it constructed from a Postfix expression?
cards.back:
• Expression Tree: A binary tree where leaf nodes are operands and internal nodes are operators.
• Construction from Postfix using Stack:
  Scan postfix expression left-to-right:
  - If Operand: Create single-node tree, push pointer to stack.
  - If Operator (op): Create operator node. Pop top node (Right Child) and second top node (Left Child). Link to operator node. Push operator node back to stack.
  - Final stack element is the root of the expression tree.
cards.formula_or_code: Leaves = Operands | Internal Nodes = Operators

cards.front: State the BST ordering invariant and describe the 3 cases of BST Node Deletion.
cards.back:
• BST Invariant: For every node X, all keys in Left(X) < X->data < all keys in Right(X).
• Deletion Cases:
  1. Node is a Leaf (0 children): Disconnect from parent and free(node).
  2. Node has 1 Child: Bypass node by linking parent directly to child; free(node).
  3. Node has 2 Children: Find Inorder Successor (minimum in right subtree) or Inorder Predecessor (max in left subtree). Copy successor's value into current node, then delete successor from right subtree (which has at most 1 child).
cards.formula_or_code: BST Invariant: Left < Root < Right | 2-Child Delete: Replace with Inorder Successor

cards.front: Define Binary Heap (Max/Min), array index mapping, and explain why Build-Heap runs in O(n) time.
cards.back:
• Definition: A Complete Binary Tree satisfying Heap Order: Max-Heap (parent ≥ children), Min-Heap (parent ≤ children).
• Array Indices (0-based): Left = 2i + 1, Right = 2i + 2, Parent = floor((i-1)/2).
• Linear Time Build-Heap Derivation:
  Calls heapify-down on non-leaves from floor(n/2)-1 down to 0.
  Total Cost = sum_{h=0}^{floor(log n)} (n / 2^(h+1)) * O(h) = (n/2) * sum_{h=0}^inf (h / 2^h) = (n/2) * 2 = O(n) linear time!
cards.formula_or_code: Build-Heap: O(n) | Insert / Extract-Max: O(log n)

cards.front: Compare Adjacency Matrix and Adjacency List representations of a graph.
cards.back:
• Adjacency Matrix: V × V 2D array M[i][j] = 1 if edge exists, else 0.
  - Space: Θ(V^2)
  - Edge Query (u, v): O(1)
  - Finding all neighbors of u: O(V)
  - Best for dense graphs (|E| ≈ |V|^2).
• Adjacency List: Array of linked lists where adj[u] lists neighbors of u.
  - Space: O(V + E) for digraphs, O(V + 2E) for undirected
  - Edge Query: O(degree(u))
  - Best for sparse graphs (|E| ≪ |V|^2).
cards.formula_or_code: Adj Matrix: O(V^2) space, O(1) query | Adj List: O(V + E) space

cards.front: Compare Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) in data structure, time complexity, and applications.
cards.back:
• BFS:
  - Data Structure: FIFO Queue + visited[] array.
  - Exploration: Layer-by-layer (radiates outward).
  - Time: O(V + E) with Adjacency List, Space: O(V).
  - Application: Shortest path in unweighted graphs, connected components.
• DFS:
  - Data Structure: LIFO Stack / Recursion + visited[] array.
  - Exploration: Deep along each branch before backtracking.
  - Time: O(V + E), Space: O(V) (call stack depth).
  - Application: Cycle detection, Topological sort, Path finding.
cards.formula_or_code: BFS = Queue (Shortest unweighted path) | DFS = Stack (Cycle detection)

cards.front: State Dijkstra's Single-Source Shortest Path algorithm, relaxation formula, complexity, and its main limitation.
cards.formula_or_code:
Relaxation: dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w(u,v))
Fails on negative edge weights!

cards.front: Compare Selection Sort and Insertion Sort with respect to best/worst time complexity, stability, and swaps.
cards.back:
• Selection Sort: Finds minimum in unsorted part, swaps with first unsorted element. Best: O(n^2), Worst: O(n^2), Avg: O(n^2). Minimal swaps O(n), In-place, UNSTABLE.
• Insertion Sort: Shifts elements greater than key one position right, inserts key in place. Best: O(n) (already sorted), Worst: O(n^2), Avg: O(n^2). Shifts O(n^2), In-place, STABLE.
cards.formula_or_code:
Selection: Best/Worst O(n^2), O(n) swaps, Unstable
Insertion: Best O(n), Worst O(n^2), Stable

cards.front: Explain Quick Sort partition mechanics and analyze its best and worst case time complexity with recurrences.
cards.back:
• Mechanism: Picks pivot, partitions array such that elements ≤ pivot are left, elements > pivot are right, recurses.
• Best Case: Pivot splits array into equal halves:
  T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) ⇒ O(n log n)
• Worst Case: Array already sorted or reverse sorted (skewed partition):
  T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) ⇒ O(n^2)
• Space: O(log n) average recursion stack, O(n) worst case.
• Mitigation: Randomized pivot or Median-of-Three.
cards.formula_or_code: Best: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) -> O(n log n) | Worst: T(n-1) + O(n) -> O(n^2)

cards.front: Compare Merge Sort and Heap Sort in terms of time complexity, auxiliary space, and stability.
cards.back:
• Merge Sort:
  - Time: Strictly O(n log n) in Best, Worst, and Average cases (T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)).
  - Auxiliary Space: O(n) auxiliary buffer array (NOT in-place).
  - Stability: STABLE.
• Heap Sort:
  - Time: Strictly O(n log n) in all cases (Build Heap O(n) + n Heapify O(log n)).
  - Auxiliary Space: O(1) (IN-PLACE).
  - Stability: UNSTABLE.
cards.formula_or_code:
Merge: O(n log n) always, O(n) space, Stable
Heap: O(n log n) always, O(1) space, Unstable

cards.front: What is Radix Sort and how does Binary Search achieve O(log n) time complexity?
cards.back:
• Radix Sort: Non-comparative integer sort processing digits from Least Significant Digit (LSD) to Most Significant Digit (MSD) using a STABLE subroutine (Counting Sort). Time: O(d · (n + k)). Runs in O(n) linear time when digit count d is constant.
• Binary Search: On a SORTED array, repeatedly compares target with middle element, halving search space: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) ⇒ O(log n).
cards.formula_or_code: Radix: O(d * (n + k)) | Binary Search: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) -> O(log n)

cards.front: Name and define the 4 common Hash Functions: Division, Mid-Square, Folding, and Digit Analysis.
cards.back:
1. Division Method: h(k) = k mod m (m should be a prime number).
2. Mid-Square Method: Square the key (k^2), extract middle r digits as address (table size m = 10^r or 2^r).
3. Folding Method:
   - Shift Folding: Divide key into equal chunks, sum chunks, take modulo m.
   - Boundary Folding: Reverse outer chunks before adding.
4. Digit Analysis: Examine statistical frequency across digit positions, select positions with most uniform distribution.
cards.formula_or_code: Division: k mod m | Mid-Square: Middle digits of k^2 | Folding: Sum chunks mod m

cards.front: Explain Linear Probing, Quadratic Probing, Double Hashing, and define Primary vs Secondary Clustering.
cards.back:
• Linear Probing: h(k, i) = (h'(k) + i) mod m. Causes Primary Clustering (contiguous blocks of filled slots grow, degrading search to O(n)).
• Quadratic Probing: h(k, i) = (h'(k) + c1·i + c2·i^2) mod m. Eliminates primary clustering; suffers from Secondary Clustering (keys with same initial hash follow identical probe sequences).
• Double Hashing: h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i · h2(k)) mod m. Completely eliminates both primary and secondary clustering.
cards.formula_or_code: Linear: (h'(k) + i) mod m | Quadratic: (h'(k) + c1*i + c2*i^2) mod m | Double: (h1 + i*h2) mod m

cards.front: Explain Separate Chaining (Open Hashing) and compare it with Open Addressing.
cards.back:
• Separate Chaining: Hash table is an array of linked list heads. Colliding keys are chained in a linked list at slot T[i].
  - Load Factor α = n / m (can exceed 1).
  - Search Time: O(1 + α).
  - Advantages: Never overflows, simple node deletion, graceful degradation.
• Open Addressing: All elements stored directly in array (α ≤ 1). Overflow occurs when table fills; deletion requires 'tombstones'.
cards.formula_or_code: Chaining: Array of Linked Lists | Search Time = O(1 + alpha)

flashcards.front: What is the distinction between Data, Data Structures, and an Abstract Data Type (ADT)?
flashcards.back:
• Data: Raw, unorganized facts or values.
• Data Structure: A specialized mathematical/logical format for organizing, storing, retrieving, and manipulating data efficiently.
• ADT: A mathematical model defined solely by its data behavior and set of operations from the user's perspective, completely independent of implementation details.
flashcards.formula_or_code: ADT = Set of Values + Set of Operations

flashcards.front: What is a Sparse Matrix? Describe its 3-Tuple representation.
flashcards.back:
• Definition: A matrix where the vast majority of elements are ZERO. Storing as a standard 2D array wastes memory and computational cycles.
• 3-Tuple Representation: Stored in a compact array of rows [row, col, value].
  - Row 0 (Metadata): [total_rows, total_cols, total_non_zero_elements].
  - Rows 1..k: [r, c, val] for each non-zero element in row-major order.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Row 0: [Rows, Cols, NonZeros] | Row i: [Row_idx, Col_idx, Value]
flashcards.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

flashcards.front: Compare Simple Transpose vs Fast Transpose of a Sparse Matrix in terms of time and space complexity.
flashcards.back:
• Simple Transpose: For each column (0 to cols-1), scans all N non-zero elements to place them in transposed order. Time: O(C × N). Space: O(1) auxiliary.
• Fast Transpose: Precomputes two auxiliary arrays:
  1. row_terms[col]: counts non-zero elements per column.
  2. starting_pos[col]: computes starting index in transposed matrix.
  Places each element in exact position in a single pass. Time: O(C + N). Space: O(C) auxiliary.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Simple: O(C * N) | Fast: O(C + N) with row_terms & starting_pos
flashcards.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

flashcards.front: Define Stack ADT, its operations, and state the Overflow & Underflow conditions in array implementation.
flashcards.back:
• Stack: LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) linear list where insertions and deletions happen only at one end (TOP).
• Operations: Push (insert), Pop (delete), Peek (inspect top).
• Array Implementation (size MAX, top initialized to -1):
  - Overflow Condition: top == MAX - 1 (cannot push onto full stack).
  - Underflow Condition: top == -1 (cannot pop from empty stack).
flashcards.formula_or_code:
Push: if(top==MAX-1) Overflow; else arr[++top]=val;
Pop: if(top==-1) Underflow; else return arr[top--];
flashcards.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

flashcards.front: How do you implement Two Stacks in a Single Array efficiently without artificial boundary collisions?
flashcards.back:
• Array arr[0..MAX-1] with two pointers:
  - Stack 1 grows from left to right: top1 initialized to -1 (Push: ++top1).
  - Stack 2 grows from right to left: top2 initialized to MAX (Push: --top2).
• Underflow:
  - Stack 1: top1 == -1
  - Stack 2: top2 == MAX
• Overflow Condition: top1 + 1 == top2 (occurs only when entire array is completely full).
flashcards.formula_or_code: Overflow: top1 + 1 == top2
flashcards.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

flashcards.front: State the algorithm rules for converting an Infix expression to Postfix using an operator stack.
flashcards.back:
1. Initialize operator stack.
2. Scan infix token left-to-right:
   - If Operand: Append directly to postfix output.
   - If '(': Push to stack.
   - If ')': Pop and append from stack until '(' is encountered; discard '('.
   - If Operator (op): While stack is non-empty and precedence(stack[top]) ≥ precedence(op) (for left-associative), pop and append. Then push op onto stack.
3. After scanning, pop all remaining operators from stack to output.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Precedence: ^ (R-to-L) > *, / (L-to-R) > +, - (L-to-R)
flashcards.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

flashcards.front: How does an Operand Stack evaluate a Postfix arithmetic expression?
flashcards.back:
1. Initialize operand stack.
2. Scan postfix expression from left-to-right:
   - If Operand: Push value onto stack.
   - If Operator (op): Pop top two operands (op2 = pop(), op1 = pop()). Compute result = op1 [op] op2. Push result back onto stack.
3. Final result is the single element remaining on stack.
(Critical: Second popped element is LEFT operand; first popped is RIGHT operand!).
flashcards.formula_or_code: op2 = pop(); op1 = pop(); push(op1 [op] op2);
flashcards.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

flashcards.front: What is the False Overflow problem in a Linear Queue, and how does a Circular Queue solve it?
flashcards.formula_or_code: Circular Full: (rear + 1) % MAX == front | Empty: front == rear
flashcards.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

flashcards.front: Define Double-Ended Queue (Deque) variants and Priority Queue.
flashcards.back:
• Deque (Double-Ended Queue): Linear list where insertion and deletion can occur at BOTH ends (front and rear).
  - Input-Restricted Deque: Insertion at one end only; deletion at both ends.
  - Output-Restricted Deque: Deletion at one end only; insertion at both ends.
• Priority Queue: Queue where each element has an assigned priority. Elements are dequeued based on priority (highest priority first), regardless of arrival order.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Deque: Insert/Delete at Front & Rear | Priority Queue: Highest priority served first
flashcards.module_title: Basic Concepts of Data Structures, Complexity Analysis & Stacks / Queues

flashcards.front: Define a Singly Linked List (SLL) node in C and compare array vs linked list memory allocation.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Node* n = (Node*)malloc(sizeof(Node)); n->data = val; n->next = NULL;
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: Give the C pointer statements for SLL Insertion and Deletion at Head.
flashcards.formula_or_code:
Insert Head: newNode->next=head; head=newNode;
Delete Head: temp=head; head=head->next; free(temp);
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: Write the 3-pointer in-place algorithm to reverse a Singly Linked List.
flashcards.formula_or_code: 3-Pointers: prev=NULL, curr=head, next=NULL; curr->next=prev
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: How are dynamic Stacks and Queues implemented using a Linked List?
flashcards.back:
• Dynamic Stack:
  - Push: Insert at Head (top) → O(1)
  - Pop: Delete from Head (top) → O(1)
  - Underflow: top == NULL
• Dynamic Queue:
  - Enqueue: Insert at Tail (rear) using rear pointer → O(1)
  - Dequeue: Delete from Head (front) using front pointer → O(1)
  - Underflow: front == NULL
flashcards.formula_or_code: Stack: Push/Pop at Head | Queue: Enqueue at Tail, Dequeue at Head
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: Describe Doubly Linked List (DLL) node structure and its advantages over Singly Linked List.
flashcards.formula_or_code: DLL Node: prev (pointer), data, next (pointer)
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: Why is representing a Circular Linked List (CLL) with a single LAST pointer superior to using a HEAD pointer?
flashcards.back:
• If represented with HEAD: Finding the tail requires traversing all n nodes (O(n)).
• If represented with LAST pointer:
  - Tail node is directly accessible: last (O(1)).
  - Head node is directly accessible: last->next (O(1)).
  - Insertion at beginning: newNode->next = last->next; last->next = newNode; (O(1)).
  - Insertion at end: newNode->next = last->next; last->next = newNode; last = newNode; (O(1)).
flashcards.formula_or_code: CLL with LAST: Head = last->next (O(1)) | Tail = last (O(1))
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: Compare First-Fit, Best-Fit, Worst-Fit, and Next-Fit dynamic storage allocation schemes.
flashcards.back:
• First-Fit: Allocates the FIRST free memory hole large enough. Fast, leaves residual fragments at beginning.
• Best-Fit: Searches entire free list to find the SMALLEST hole ≥ requested size. Minimizes wasted space per allocation, but creates many tiny unusable fragments.
• Worst-Fit: Searches entire free list to allocate the LARGEST available hole. Leftover fragment is large and often reusable, but destroys large memory blocks.
• Next-Fit: Variant of First-Fit; starts searching from location of previous allocation.
flashcards.formula_or_code: First-Fit: Fastest | Best-Fit: Smallest fitting | Worst-Fit: Largest hole
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: Differentiate between Internal Fragmentation and External Fragmentation with causes and remedies.
flashcards.back:
• Internal Fragmentation: Memory allocated to a process is slightly larger than requested. The unused portion inside the allocated partition is wasted.
  - Cause: Fixed partitioning or block-size rounding.
• External Fragmentation: Total free memory across the system is sufficient to satisfy a request, but the memory is fragmented into non-contiguous scattered holes.
  - Cause: Dynamic variable-block allocation and deallocation.
  - Remedy: Memory Compaction / Paging.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Internal: Wasted inside block | External: Wasted between blocks
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: Explain the Mark-and-Sweep garbage collection algorithm and Memory Compaction.
flashcards.back:
• Mark-and-Sweep GC:
  1. Mark Phase: Starts from Root Set (stack variables, globals), traverses all reachable objects via pointer graph, setting a 'visited/marked' bit = 1.
  2. Sweep Phase: Scans the entire heap linearly. Unmarked objects (bit = 0) are garbage collected and returned to free pool; marked bits are reset to 0.
• Memory Compaction: Relocates all live surviving objects to one contiguous end of the heap, updating all reference pointers, producing a single large contiguous free memory block.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Phase 1: Mark reachable from roots | Phase 2: Sweep unmarked to free list
flashcards.module_title: Linked Lists, Dynamic ADTs & Memory Management

flashcards.front: State the key mathematical properties of Binary Trees (max nodes at level i, max nodes in height h, min height with n nodes).
flashcards.back:
1. Max nodes at level i (root at level 0): 2^i
2. Max nodes in a binary tree of height h: 2^(h+1) - 1
3. Min height with n nodes: h_min = ceil(log2(n+1)) - 1
4. Strict / Full Binary Tree: Nodes have either 0 or 2 children.
5. Complete Binary Tree: All levels filled except possibly last (nodes pushed left).
6. Perfect Binary Tree: All interior nodes have 2 children, all leaves at same level.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Max nodes at level i = 2^i | Max nodes in height h = 2^(h+1) - 1
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: Prove that in any non-empty binary tree, the number of leaf nodes (n0) is one more than the number of degree-2 nodes (n2): n0 = n2 + 1.
flashcards.back:
Let n = total nodes, e = total edges.
1. Every edge points to a child, so e = n - 1.
2. In terms of node degrees (n0, n1, n2):
   e = 0·n0 + 1·n1 + 2·n2 = n1 + 2·n2.
3. Equating:
   n - 1 = n1 + 2·n2
4. Since n = n0 + n1 + n2:
   (n0 + n1 + n2) - 1 = n1 + 2·n2
   n0 - 1 = n2  ⇒  n0 = n2 + 1  ■
flashcards.formula_or_code: Theorem: n_0 = n_2 + 1
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: Define Inorder, Preorder, Postorder, and Level-Order traversals of a Binary Tree.
flashcards.back:
• Inorder (L-N-R): Traverse Left Subtree → Visit Node → Traverse Right Subtree (Sorted order in BST).
• Preorder (N-L-R): Visit Node → Traverse Left Subtree → Traverse Right Subtree (Used for copying/prefix expressions).
• Postorder (L-R-N): Traverse Left Subtree → Traverse Right Subtree → Visit Node (Used for tree deletion/postfix evaluation).
• Level-Order: Breadth-first level-by-level traversal using a FIFO Queue.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Inorder: LNR | Preorder: NLR | Postorder: LRN | Level-Order: Queue
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: Why is Inorder traversal MANDATORY to uniquely reconstruct a binary tree along with Preorder or Postorder?
flashcards.back:
• Preorder/Postorder indicates the Root node (first in Preorder, last in Postorder), but cannot distinguish whether remaining elements belong to the left or right subtree.
• Inorder establishes the boundary: finding the root in Inorder divides elements into Left Subtree (elements to the left of root) and Right Subtree (elements to the right of root).
• Preorder + Postorder CANNOT construct a unique tree (ambiguity arises with single-child nodes).
flashcards.formula_or_code: Unique Tree = Inorder + Preorder OR Inorder + Postorder
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: What is an Expression Tree and how is it constructed from a Postfix expression?
flashcards.back:
• Expression Tree: A binary tree where leaf nodes are operands and internal nodes are operators.
• Construction from Postfix using Stack:
  Scan postfix expression left-to-right:
  - If Operand: Create single-node tree, push pointer to stack.
  - If Operator (op): Create operator node. Pop top node (Right Child) and second top node (Left Child). Link to operator node. Push operator node back to stack.
  - Final stack element is the root of the expression tree.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Leaves = Operands | Internal Nodes = Operators
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: State the BST ordering invariant and describe the 3 cases of BST Node Deletion.
flashcards.back:
• BST Invariant: For every node X, all keys in Left(X) < X->data < all keys in Right(X).
• Deletion Cases:
  1. Node is a Leaf (0 children): Disconnect from parent and free(node).
  2. Node has 1 Child: Bypass node by linking parent directly to child; free(node).
  3. Node has 2 Children: Find Inorder Successor (minimum in right subtree) or Inorder Predecessor (max in left subtree). Copy successor's value into current node, then delete successor from right subtree (which has at most 1 child).
flashcards.formula_or_code: BST Invariant: Left < Root < Right | 2-Child Delete: Replace with Inorder Successor
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: Define Binary Heap (Max/Min), array index mapping, and explain why Build-Heap runs in O(n) time.
flashcards.back:
• Definition: A Complete Binary Tree satisfying Heap Order: Max-Heap (parent ≥ children), Min-Heap (parent ≤ children).
• Array Indices (0-based): Left = 2i + 1, Right = 2i + 2, Parent = floor((i-1)/2).
• Linear Time Build-Heap Derivation:
  Calls heapify-down on non-leaves from floor(n/2)-1 down to 0.
  Total Cost = sum_{h=0}^{floor(log n)} (n / 2^(h+1)) * O(h) = (n/2) * sum_{h=0}^inf (h / 2^h) = (n/2) * 2 = O(n) linear time!
flashcards.formula_or_code: Build-Heap: O(n) | Insert / Extract-Max: O(log n)
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: Compare Adjacency Matrix and Adjacency List representations of a graph.
flashcards.back:
• Adjacency Matrix: V × V 2D array M[i][j] = 1 if edge exists, else 0.
  - Space: Θ(V^2)
  - Edge Query (u, v): O(1)
  - Finding all neighbors of u: O(V)
  - Best for dense graphs (|E| ≈ |V|^2).
• Adjacency List: Array of linked lists where adj[u] lists neighbors of u.
  - Space: O(V + E) for digraphs, O(V + 2E) for undirected
  - Edge Query: O(degree(u))
  - Best for sparse graphs (|E| ≪ |V|^2).
flashcards.formula_or_code: Adj Matrix: O(V^2) space, O(1) query | Adj List: O(V + E) space
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: Compare Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) in data structure, time complexity, and applications.
flashcards.back:
• BFS:
  - Data Structure: FIFO Queue + visited[] array.
  - Exploration: Layer-by-layer (radiates outward).
  - Time: O(V + E) with Adjacency List, Space: O(V).
  - Application: Shortest path in unweighted graphs, connected components.
• DFS:
  - Data Structure: LIFO Stack / Recursion + visited[] array.
  - Exploration: Deep along each branch before backtracking.
  - Time: O(V + E), Space: O(V) (call stack depth).
  - Application: Cycle detection, Topological sort, Path finding.
flashcards.formula_or_code: BFS = Queue (Shortest unweighted path) | DFS = Stack (Cycle detection)
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: State Dijkstra's Single-Source Shortest Path algorithm, relaxation formula, complexity, and its main limitation.
flashcards.formula_or_code:
Relaxation: dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w(u,v))
Fails on negative edge weights!
flashcards.module_title: Trees & Graphs

flashcards.front: Compare Selection Sort and Insertion Sort with respect to best/worst time complexity, stability, and swaps.
flashcards.back:
• Selection Sort: Finds minimum in unsorted part, swaps with first unsorted element. Best: O(n^2), Worst: O(n^2), Avg: O(n^2). Minimal swaps O(n), In-place, UNSTABLE.
• Insertion Sort: Shifts elements greater than key one position right, inserts key in place. Best: O(n) (already sorted), Worst: O(n^2), Avg: O(n^2). Shifts O(n^2), In-place, STABLE.
flashcards.formula_or_code:
Selection: Best/Worst O(n^2), O(n) swaps, Unstable
Insertion: Best O(n), Worst O(n^2), Stable
flashcards.module_title: Sorting, Searching & Hashing

flashcards.front: Explain Quick Sort partition mechanics and analyze its best and worst case time complexity with recurrences.
flashcards.back:
• Mechanism: Picks pivot, partitions array such that elements ≤ pivot are left, elements > pivot are right, recurses.
• Best Case: Pivot splits array into equal halves:
  T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) ⇒ O(n log n)
• Worst Case: Array already sorted or reverse sorted (skewed partition):
  T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) ⇒ O(n^2)
• Space: O(log n) average recursion stack, O(n) worst case.
• Mitigation: Randomized pivot or Median-of-Three.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Best: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) -> O(n log n) | Worst: T(n-1) + O(n) -> O(n^2)
flashcards.module_title: Sorting, Searching & Hashing

flashcards.front: Compare Merge Sort and Heap Sort in terms of time complexity, auxiliary space, and stability.
flashcards.back:
• Merge Sort:
  - Time: Strictly O(n log n) in Best, Worst, and Average cases (T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)).
  - Auxiliary Space: O(n) auxiliary buffer array (NOT in-place).
  - Stability: STABLE.
• Heap Sort:
  - Time: Strictly O(n log n) in all cases (Build Heap O(n) + n Heapify O(log n)).
  - Auxiliary Space: O(1) (IN-PLACE).
  - Stability: UNSTABLE.
flashcards.formula_or_code:
Merge: O(n log n) always, O(n) space, Stable
Heap: O(n log n) always, O(1) space, Unstable
flashcards.module_title: Sorting, Searching & Hashing

flashcards.front: What is Radix Sort and how does Binary Search achieve O(log n) time complexity?
flashcards.back:
• Radix Sort: Non-comparative integer sort processing digits from Least Significant Digit (LSD) to Most Significant Digit (MSD) using a STABLE subroutine (Counting Sort). Time: O(d · (n + k)). Runs in O(n) linear time when digit count d is constant.
• Binary Search: On a SORTED array, repeatedly compares target with middle element, halving search space: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) ⇒ O(log n).
flashcards.formula_or_code: Radix: O(d * (n + k)) | Binary Search: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) -> O(log n)
flashcards.module_title: Sorting, Searching & Hashing

flashcards.front: Name and define the 4 common Hash Functions: Division, Mid-Square, Folding, and Digit Analysis.
flashcards.back:
1. Division Method: h(k) = k mod m (m should be a prime number).
2. Mid-Square Method: Square the key (k^2), extract middle r digits as address (table size m = 10^r or 2^r).
3. Folding Method:
   - Shift Folding: Divide key into equal chunks, sum chunks, take modulo m.
   - Boundary Folding: Reverse outer chunks before adding.
4. Digit Analysis: Examine statistical frequency across digit positions, select positions with most uniform distribution.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Division: k mod m | Mid-Square: Middle digits of k^2 | Folding: Sum chunks mod m
flashcards.module_title: Sorting, Searching & Hashing

flashcards.front: Explain Linear Probing, Quadratic Probing, Double Hashing, and define Primary vs Secondary Clustering.
flashcards.back:
• Linear Probing: h(k, i) = (h'(k) + i) mod m. Causes Primary Clustering (contiguous blocks of filled slots grow, degrading search to O(n)).
• Quadratic Probing: h(k, i) = (h'(k) + c1·i + c2·i^2) mod m. Eliminates primary clustering; suffers from Secondary Clustering (keys with same initial hash follow identical probe sequences).
• Double Hashing: h(k, i) = (h1(k) + i · h2(k)) mod m. Completely eliminates both primary and secondary clustering.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Linear: (h'(k) + i) mod m | Quadratic: (h'(k) + c1*i + c2*i^2) mod m | Double: (h1 + i*h2) mod m
flashcards.module_title: Sorting, Searching & Hashing

flashcards.front: Explain Separate Chaining (Open Hashing) and compare it with Open Addressing.
flashcards.back:
• Separate Chaining: Hash table is an array of linked list heads. Colliding keys are chained in a linked list at slot T[i].
  - Load Factor α = n / m (can exceed 1).
  - Search Time: O(1 + α).
  - Advantages: Never overflows, simple node deletion, graceful degradation.
• Open Addressing: All elements stored directly in array (α ≤ 1). Overflow occurs when table fills; deletion requires 'tombstones'.
flashcards.formula_or_code: Chaining: Array of Linked Lists | Search Time = O(1 + alpha)
flashcards.module_title: Sorting, Searching & Hashing
